newsitem.title: UK: UK may hurry in new law if strikes worsen - Lang.
newsitem.headline: UK may hurry in new law if strikes worsen - Lang.

text.p: The government could hurry in proposals to ban strikes in public-sector monopolies if industrial action escalates, Trade Secretary Ian Lang said on Wednesday.

Speaking to reporters after outlining plans that would allow striking unions to be sued for damages, Lang said it was possible that the government would decide to legislate before the end of the current parliament next April.
"If industrial relations deteriorate, we may accelerate our plans," Lang, who unveiled his proposals as a result of rail, post and London Underground strikes this summer, added.
He said he would publish a consultation paper when parliament returns next week from its summer break and ask for comments over the next two to three months.
If the law is passed, Lang said he did not expect many cases to come before the courts, partly because plaintiffs would have to be able to prove substantial losses directly due to the strike.

Moreover, Lang said, the law would deter unions who "irresponsibly use the public as pawns" from going on strike in the first place. "It creates another hurdle the union must clear in contemplating strike action," he said.
Key to the proposal is the concept of "proportionality" --if a strike's effects are disproportionately damaging to the public, the union responsible could be sued by the employer and the customer.
An example could be a hospital that is closed down by a strike in a town where there are no alternative emergency services, or a house that burns down because the fire brigade has gone on strike.
But Lang said the government would not seek to define proportionality. This would be left to the courts, which would gradually build up a body of case law.
Asked whether a strike ban would constitute an infringement of trade unionists' civil right to withdraw their labour, Lang replied: "We're defending the civil rights of the public."
